extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and other practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO in trademark (and other non-patent) matters; counsel involved in USPTO enrollment/discipline and applicants for reinstatement
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing competent trademark practice before the USPTO, misconduct definitions (e.g., misrepresentation, aiding unauthorized practice), account/signature obligations, and the consequences/procedures for exclusion on consent and reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 — Competent representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes understanding and complying with the U.S. Counsel Rule, USPTO trademark signature rules, USPTO.gov account rules, not sponsoring accounts for unauthorized individuals, having adequate training in trademark practice, and safeguarding account credentials. The OED Director treated failures in these areas (e.g., practicing without adequate training, sharing account access) as violations of §11.101.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — Assistance in unauthorized practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not assist another in practicing law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of prohibited assistance include allowing a non-practitioner to create/use a USPTO.gov account in the practitioner's name, accepting compensation for others' use of attorney credentials/signature, sponsoring accounts for non-practitioners who are not supervised/employed by the practitioner, failing to supervise or monitor sponsored users, and not searching USPTO records to detect unauthorized filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — Misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to engage in conduct involving misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes allowing other persons to enter the practitioner's signature on trademark documents that identify the practitioner as the named signatory and attorney of record. The document cites case law and prior orders treating such false signatory information as misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — Prejudicial conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes permitting others to create/use a USPTO.gov account in the practitioner's name, sharing account access resulting in impermissible filings, sponsoring accounts for non-practitioners who then engage in unauthorized practice, allowing others to enter the practitioner's signature on filings, and failing to search for or detect unauthorized filings — all of which may prejudice the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i) — Conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catch-all standard applied where acts/omissions related to trademark representation (even if not fitting other specific misconduct categories) nonetheless reflect adversely on fitness to practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rules (37 C.F.R. § 2.193 and related TMEP §611.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signature requirements for trademark filings: the person(s) identified as the signatory must personally sign the document; authority to sign may not be delegated; no one may use document-signing software to enter or electronically generate someone else's signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trademark submission signed by someone other than the named signatory is improperly executed and cannot be relied upon to support registration. A signature that does not meet the 'personally signed'/'personally entered' requirement may jeopardize the validity of an application or registration. Examples and case citations (In re Yusha Zhang; In re Ste/Core) emphasize that these rules are substantive, not merely technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b) — Prohibition on false/misleading information and requirement of reasonable inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting documents that include false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information violates §11.18(b)(1); submitting without a reasonable inquiry into the factual basis violates §11.18(b)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: false or misleading domicile, attorney information, signatory information (e.g., named signatory did not personally sign), applicant information, or claims of use. Submitting such information to circumvent USPTO rules, or without evidentiary support, is improper and may constitute an intent to mislead or circumvent rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO.gov Terms of Use and Verified Account Agreement obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Users of USPTO systems are bound by Terms of Use and the Trademark Verified USPTO.gov Account Agreement; accounts are limited to the registered individual who is responsible for all activities under that account and any sponsored accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration/use is limited to the individual account holder; users must maintain confidentiality of login information; sharing credentials is prohibited; registered individual bears responsibility for activities occurring under the account and sponsored accounts. Violations may also implicate other rules (e.g., §2.193 and §11.18(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsorship responsibilities for USPTO.gov accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: When sponsoring another person's USPTO.gov account, the sponsor must truthfully certify that the sponsored individual works under the sponsor's direction and control and must monitor sponsored accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False certifications of supervision or employment are misconduct. Sponsors are expected to implement means to monitor or periodically review whether sponsored accounts are being used and to search public records for filings listing them as attorney of record; failure to do so can allow unauthorized use of the sponsor's credentials and may be disciplinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to supervise, monitor, and periodically check public records
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who associate with non-attorneys or third parties must supervise and monitor those persons and periodically check USPTO public records to detect unauthorized filings made under the practitioner's credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office expects practitioners to implement supervision/monitoring and to use USPTO search tools to identify applications/registrations listing them as attorney of record. Failing to supervise or to check public records enabled thousands of filings under the respondent's account without her review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Resignation requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit of resignation submitted for exclusion on consent must comply with §11.27(a): consent must be freely and voluntarily rendered, the practitioner must be aware of pending investigations and consequences, and must acknowledge relevant facts and regulatory consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The affidavit should acknowledge voluntariness (no coercion), awareness of an investigation and the facts gathered, and understanding of the legal/factual consequences of consenting to exclusion. Compliance with §11.27(b) and related regs is required for approval by the USPTO Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement presumption upon consent exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.60 implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who consents to exclusion may be required, upon any future reinstatement application under §11.60, to accept certain presumptions regarding the facts and inability to defend against the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director may conclusively presume the investigation facts are true for reinstatement purposes and that the practitioner could not have successfully defended against the allegations embodied in the OED Director's opinion. Practitioners must acknowledge this as part of consenting to exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice requirements following disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director will publish the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and issue a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary orders and notices include factual summary of the conduct, procedural disposition (e.g., exclusion on consent), and reference to statutory/regulatory authority. Publication is part of the disciplinary process and public record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions and obligations while excluded (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.59, 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded practitioner must comply with §11.58 and related provisions; the USPTO may disable or suspend USPTO.gov accounts; the excluded practitioner is prohibited from applying for, obtaining, using, verifying, or sponsoring USPTO verified accounts for preparing or filing documents until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prohibitions include: not applying for or activating USPTO.gov accounts for filing; not obtaining or being added to such accounts; not verifying other persons' credentials for account purposes; not sponsoring accounts; and not assisting others in accessing/using USPTO systems to prepare/file documents. The practitioner is responsible for any request to reactivate disabled accounts and must comply with reinstatement procedures in §11.60.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of familiarity with USPTO trademark resources (TMEP and website guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are reasonably expected to know applicable trademark prosecution/signature rules, provisions of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct implicated by trademark representation, and potential disciplinary consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO publishes the Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure (TMEP) and other trademark guidance (e.g., tmep.uspto.gov, uspto.gov/trademarks). TMEP §611.01 is cited for clear guidance on signature rules; practitioners are expected to consult these resources and keep current with updates.
